entries.lesson_core_move: Map each real-valued time instant \(t\) to its signal value \(x(t)\), using the function viewpoint to interpret continuous-time signal notation before graphs, piecewise definitions, support, symmetry, and basic parameters.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Continuous-Time Signals as Functions
sections.learning_goal: State that a continuous-time signal is a function that assigns a value \(x(t)\) to each real time \(t\), and make the input-output relationship explicit.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; keep the opening focused on symbolic function notation so graph reading remains reserved for the next lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make the target move explicit: a continuous-time signal is a rule that takes a real-valued time input \(t\) and returns a signal value \(x(t)\).
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple rule such as \(x(t)=2t+1\) and show that choosing \(t=3\) produces the single value \(x(3)=7\).
paragraph_plan: Introduce continuous time as allowing any real time value, not only whole-number time indices.
Define a continuous-time signal as a function of time and identify \(t\) as the input and \(x(t)\) as the output.
State the core move: choose a time, substitute that time into the signal rule, and interpret the result as the signal value at that time.
Use one simple substitution to demonstrate the mapping from a time instant to a signal value.
Preview that this same function viewpoint will make graphs, piecewise rules, support, symmetry, and parameters meaningful in later lessons.
display_math_plan: Show one base-case substitution, for example \(x(t)=2t+1\) and \(x(3)=2(3)+1=7\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Tutorial only; do not include practice questions here. Keep the explanation to the minimum effective dose needed before the first notation-reading example.

sections.section_title: Interpreting \(x(t)\) as a Time-to-Value Rule
sections.learning_goal: Interpret notation such as \(x(2)=5\) as a statement that a specific time input maps to a specific signal value.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the section should train symbolic notation reading, not graph inspection.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered pair or short statement identifying the time input and signal value
question_policy.practice_question_model: In the statement \(x(-3)=8\), what is the time input and what is the signal value?
distractor_plan: For generated feedback, target common errors such as swapping the time input and output value.
Flag interpretations that treat \(x(t)\) as multiplication by \(x\) instead of function notation.
Flag answers that identify only the value in parentheses or only the value after the equals sign.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the statement \(x(2)=5\), identify the time input and the signal value.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the number inside the parentheses is the input time and the value after the equals sign is the signal value at that time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the tutorial's general definition to reading one concrete signal notation statement without computing from a formula.
solution_step_plan: Point to the value inside the parentheses and label it as the chosen time.
Point to the value after the equals sign and label it as the output of the signal at that time.
Restate the notation as a mapping from the time input to the signal value.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive, negative, and zero time inputs.
Use positive, negative, and zero signal values.
Alternate between asking for labels and asking for the complete time-to-value statement.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section as notation reading only; do not introduce graphs, tables, support, symmetry, or piecewise definitions.

sections.section_title: Finding \(x(t_0)\) at a Specific Time
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate a symbolic signal rule at a specified time by substituting \(t_0\) for \(t\) and simplifying the result.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the mathematical work is substitution into a compact formula.

question_policy.answer_format: number or simplified expression
distractor_plan: For generated feedback, target substituting the wrong time value into the formula.
Flag arithmetic errors after the correct substitution setup.
Flag answers that rewrite the formula but never evaluate at the requested time.

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate the full substitution workflow from the requested time \(t_0=4\) to the computed signal value.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds computation by substituting a specified time into a simple signal rule.
solution_step_plan: Identify the requested input time from the notation \(x(4)\).
Substitute \(4\) for every occurrence of \(t\) in the rule.
Simplify the arithmetic carefully.
State the final value as the signal value at that time.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the coefficient of \(t\).
Vary the constant offset.
Use small positive, negative, and zero requested times.
Keep formulas linear to preserve the single new wrinkle.

sections.handoff_notes: Use subgoal labels around identify, substitute, simplify, and interpret. Keep the examples close to the worked prompt so practice reinforces the exact move.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Signal at Non-Integer Times
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same substitution move when the time input is fractional or decimal, reinforcing that continuous time uses real-valued instants.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the point is that non-integer real inputs are handled by the same symbolic substitution process.

question_policy.answer_format: number or simplified expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let \(x(t)=6t-1\). Find \(x\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\).
distractor_plan: For generated feedback, target replacing \(t\) with only the numerator or only the denominator of the fraction.
Flag missing parentheses around the substituted non-integer input.
Flag fraction or decimal arithmetic errors after the correct substitution setup.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let \(x(t)=4t+1\). Find \(x\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a fractional time is still a valid continuous-time input and is evaluated by the same substitution process.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same substitution rule but changes the time input from an integer to a non-integer real value.
solution_step_plan: Identify the requested non-integer time input.
Substitute the entire fractional input for \(t\), using parentheses.
Simplify the product involving the fraction.
State the resulting signal value and connect it back to the continuous-time viewpoint.
practice_variation_axes: Use simple fractional inputs such as \(1/2\), \(1/3\), and \(3/2\).
Use terminating decimal inputs only when arithmetic remains light.
Include occasional negative non-integer inputs after the basic fraction case is clear.
Keep formulas simple enough that the non-integer input is the only meaningful wrinkle.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not use a graph to motivate non-integer time; the instructional target is that the domain of \(t\) is real-valued and the substitution process does not change.

sections.section_title: Reading a Signal Rule Over All Real Time
sections.learning_goal: Interpret a signal formula as assigning values to every real time in its domain, rather than as only one computed value.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the closing section should consolidate the function-rule viewpoint without shifting into graph reading.

question_policy.answer_format: short statement plus ordered list of requested signal values
question_policy.practice_question_model: For \(x(t)=2t^2+1\), describe what the rule assigns to an arbitrary time \(t\), then find \(x(-1)\), \(x(0)\), and \(x(2)\).
distractor_plan: For generated feedback, target treating the formula as one isolated value instead of a rule for every real time.
Flag answers that evaluate only one of the requested times.
Flag sign errors when substituting negative inputs, especially in squared terms.
Flag responses that list values without pairing them to their time inputs.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For \(x(t)=t^2-1\), describe what the rule assigns to an arbitrary time \(t\), then find \(x(-1)\), \(x(0)\), and \(x(2)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how several single-time evaluations reveal that the formula is a complete time-to-value rule over real time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Broadens from one requested input to reading a signal rule as a complete mapping that can be evaluated at any real time.
solution_step_plan: Restate the formula as a rule that takes an arbitrary real time \(t\) and returns \(t^2-1\).
Evaluate the rule at the first requested time and pair that time with its value.
Repeat the substitution for the remaining requested times.
Organize the results as time-to-value mappings.
Conclude that the formula defines the signal across real time, not just at the sampled inputs.
practice_variation_axes: Vary between simple linear and simple quadratic rules.
Ask for two or three specific time evaluations after the general rule statement.
Include a mix of negative, zero, positive, integer, and simple fractional inputs.
Keep all formulas single-rule, not piecewise, so the next lesson sequence remains clean.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this as the lesson-level consolidation step: connect individual evaluations into the durable function viewpoint, but do not ask students to draw, read, or infer a graph.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine \(x(t_0)\) from a continuous-time signal graph by locating the specified time on the horizontal axis and reading the corresponding vertical value.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Reading Signal Values from Graphs
sections.learning_goal: Make explicit that a graph of \(x(t)\) gives signal value by horizontal time coordinate and vertical signal coordinate.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Create a clean continuous-time signal graph with horizontal axis labeled \(t\), vertical axis labeled \(x(t)\), one marked time \(t_0\), and a guide from that time to the plotted curve and then to the vertical value \(x(t_0)\).
visual_elements: vertical guide from \(t_0\) to the curve
horizontal guide from the curve to \(x(t_0)\)
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a simple non-decorative coordinate plot with clear tick marks and labels; the visual should reduce load by showing the read-across/read-up procedure.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Tell the student exactly how to read \(x(t_0)\): find \(t_0\) on the horizontal axis, move to the signal graph, and read the corresponding vertical value.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A single marked time on a clean graph where the point on the signal lies exactly on a grid intersection.
paragraph_plan: Remind the student that a continuous-time signal is a function of time, so a graph pairs each time \(t\) with a value \(x(t)\).
State the three-step reading procedure: find the time, move vertically to the graph, then read the vertical coordinate.
Use the tutorial image to show the marked time \(t_0\), the point on the signal, and the read-off value \(x(t_0)\).
Warn that the horizontal coordinate is the input time and the vertical coordinate is the signal value; the answer to \(x(t_0)\) is the height, not \(t_0\).
display_math_plan: Show the notation \(x(t_0)=\text{the vertical value of the graph at time }t_0\).
Show one compact read-off statement such as \(x(2)=3\) tied to the tutorial image.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section direct and visual; do not introduce support, symmetry, amplitude, offset, duration, or piecewise notation.

sections.section_title: Reading a Signal Value at a Marked Time
sections.learning_goal: Read \(x(t_0)\) when the requested time is explicitly marked on the graph and the value is easy to see.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Use simple continuous-time signal plots where the requested time is a labeled tick mark and the point on the signal lies on a clear grid value.
visual_elements: labeled time tick for the requested input
visible grid or tick marks for the vertical value
no extra annotations that reveal the answer
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Generate one graph for the worked example and varied but closely matched graphs for follow-up questions; keep values small integers.

question_policy.answer_format: one numeric signal value
question_policy.practice_question_model: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(-1)\), where \(-1\) is a labeled tick and the graph height there is a small integer.
distractor_plan: Use the horizontal time coordinate as one distractor.
Use the signal value at an adjacent marked time as one distractor.
Use the negative of the correct value when sign confusion is plausible.
Use zero as a distractor when the graph crosses or approaches the axis nearby.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(2)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the value of \(x(2)\) is the vertical coordinate of the graph at \(t=2\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active application after the tutorial, using a marked time and an integer-valued height.
solution_step_plan: Locate \(t=2\) on the horizontal axis.
Move vertically from \(t=2\) to the graph.
Read the height of the graph at that point.
State the result in function notation as \(x(2)=\) the read-off value.
practice_variation_axes: change the requested marked time
change the graph shape while keeping the value on a grid line
use positive or negative time values
use positive or negative signal values

sections.handoff_notes: This section should feel like a direct mirror of the tutorial image, with the student practicing the basic read-off move.

sections.section_title: Reading a Signal Value Between Marked Times
sections.learning_goal: Read \(x(t_0)\) when the requested time lies between labeled ticks but the graph still determines a clear vertical value.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Use signal plots with a straight segment or clearly drawn curve between labeled time ticks, with the requested time at an unlabeled but grid-aligned position such as halfway between two ticks.
visual_elements: clear signal segment passing through the requested time
grid lines sufficient to read the vertical value
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The graph should make the value readable by inspection; avoid requiring algebraic interpolation beyond reading a plotted height.

question_policy.answer_format: one numeric signal value
question_policy.practice_question_model: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(1.5)\), where \(1.5\) lies halfway between marked ticks and the graph has a clear height there.
distractor_plan: Use the value at the left neighboring tick.
Use the value at the right neighboring tick.
Use the requested time value as a distractor.
Use a nearby vertical grid value to catch imprecise reading.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(1.5)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to read the graph at a time between labeled ticks without changing the basic horizontal-then-vertical procedure.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The time is no longer a labeled tick, but the value is still read directly from the graph.
solution_step_plan: Find where \(t=1.5\) sits between \(t=1\) and \(t=2\) on the horizontal axis.
Move vertically from that time to the plotted signal.
Read the vertical coordinate at the intersection.
Write the result as \(x(1.5)=\) the read-off value.
practice_variation_axes: use half-integer or other grid-aligned times
vary whether the signal segment is increasing or decreasing
use positive or negative read-off values
keep the requested point visually unambiguous

sections.handoff_notes: Do not turn this into slope calculation or line-equation work; the target move remains reading the plotted value.

sections.section_title: Reading a Signal Value at an Endpoint or Breakpoint
sections.learning_goal: Read \(x(t_0)\) at a graph endpoint or breakpoint by using the included plotted point rather than a nearby open point or neighboring segment.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Use continuous-time signal graphs with a breakpoint or endpoint shown using open and closed dots, where the requested time has one included value and one excluded nearby value.
visual_elements: open circle at an excluded endpoint value
closed dot at the actual value of the signal
requested breakpoint time labeled on the horizontal axis
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use open and closed endpoints clearly; the correct answer should be the closed-dot vertical coordinate at the requested time.

question_policy.answer_format: one numeric signal value
question_policy.practice_question_model: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(0)\), where the graph has an open circle at one height and a closed dot at another height at \(t=0\).
distractor_plan: Use the open-circle height as the main distractor.
Use the value approached from the neighboring segment.
Use the breakpoint time value as a distractor.
Use zero if the breakpoint lies on or near an axis.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(1)\) at the breakpoint.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the signal value at a breakpoint is the vertical coordinate of the included point at that exact time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The requested time is visually ambiguous unless the student attends to which endpoint is included.
solution_step_plan: Locate the breakpoint time on the horizontal axis.
Identify the closed dot or included point at that time.
Ignore any open circle or excluded endpoint at the same time.
Read the vertical coordinate of the included point and state \(x(1)=\) that value.
practice_variation_axes: move the breakpoint to different time values
swap which side has the included endpoint
vary the vertical gap between open and closed points
include endpoints at positive, negative, or zero times

sections.handoff_notes: This section prepares for endpoint conditions in piecewise definitions while staying inside the graph-reading move.

sections.section_title: Reading a Zero Signal Value from the Time Axis
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that \(x(t_0)=0\) when the graph is on the horizontal time axis at the requested time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Use signal plots where the requested time corresponds to a point on the horizontal time axis, making the vertical value zero.
visual_elements: signal curve or segment touching or crossing the horizontal axis
requested time labeled below the axis
clear indication that the signal point lies on \(x(t)=0\)
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the target as reading one value, not identifying an interval of zero values; question images should vary whether the graph crosses, touches, or lies briefly on the axis.

question_policy.answer_format: one numeric signal value
question_policy.practice_question_model: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(3)\), where the plotted signal passes through the horizontal axis at \(t=3\).
distractor_plan: Use the requested time coordinate as a distractor.
Use a nearby positive signal value.
Use a nearby negative signal value.
Use the value at an adjacent tick where the graph is not on the axis.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph of \(x(t)\) to find \(x(3)\) when the graph is on the time axis at \(t=3\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a point on the horizontal time axis has vertical coordinate zero, so the signal value there is zero.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The same read-off procedure now produces the special value \(0\), preparing students to notice zero values before the later support-and-zero-regions lesson.
solution_step_plan: Locate \(t=3\) on the horizontal axis.
Move to the plotted signal at that time.
Notice that the graph point lies on the horizontal time axis.
State that the vertical coordinate is \(0\), so \(x(3)=0\).
practice_variation_axes: use different times where the graph crosses the axis
use a graph that touches the axis without crossing
use a short flat segment on the axis while asking for one specified time
include nearby nonzero values to preserve the need to read the requested time

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the focus on reading a single zero value from the graph; do not ask for full support or zero-region intervals.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert graphical or functional continuous-time signal descriptions into piecewise definitions by assigning each time interval its correct expression and boundary condition.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Piecewise Signal Definitions
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that a piecewise continuous-time signal definition assigns different formulas to different time intervals, with each formula paired to the condition that tells when it applies.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for the tutorial. The notation itself is the object of instruction, and a decorative signal plot would add load before the conversion examples begin.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the structure and purpose of piecewise signal notation: one expression per interval, with boundary conditions that determine which expression gives \(x(t)\) at each time.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A two-piece signal with one constant value on \(0 \le t < 2\) and another constant value on \(2 \le t \le 4\).
paragraph_plan: Connect the prior skill of reading signal values to the need for a written rule that describes the whole signal, not just one sampled time.
State that a piecewise definition writes several expressions in one brace and attaches a time condition to each expression.
Explain that the conditions should split the time axis into the intervals where the corresponding expression is valid.
Emphasize endpoint conditions: use inequalities consistently so a boundary time is assigned to the intended piece and is not accidentally omitted or duplicated.
Preview that later sections convert flat graph pieces, sloped graph pieces, endpoint markings, verbal interval rules, and otherwise cases into the same piecewise format.
display_math_plan: Show a generic two-piece structure such as \(x(t)=\begin{cases}\text{expression 1},&\text{condition 1}\\ \text{expression 2},&\text{condition 2}\end{cases}\).
Show the base case \(x(t)=\begin{cases}1,&0\le t<2\\3,&2\le t\le4\end{cases}\), with a short note that the expressions are values and the conditions are time intervals.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section as direct instruction only. Do not include practice questions here; the active practice begins with the first worked example and mirrored questions.

sections.section_title: Writing a Piecewise Definition from Constant Graph Segments
sections.learning_goal: Convert a graph made of horizontal signal segments into a piecewise definition by reading each interval's constant value and writing the matching time condition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean continuous-time signal plot on a coordinate plane with horizontal axis labeled \(t\), vertical axis labeled \(x(t)\), and two or three horizontal constant segments over marked time intervals.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
marked breakpoints on the time axis
clear endpoint dots only where interval membership matters
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the image as mathematical data, not decoration. Keep values and breakpoints visually unambiguous, and avoid sloped or curved segments in this section.

question_policy.answer_format: A complete piecewise formula for \(x(t)\), with each constant expression paired to the correct interval inequality.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows \(x(t)=2\) for \(0\le t<3\) and \(x(t)=-1\) for \(3\le t\le5\). Write a piecewise definition for \(x(t)\).
distractor_plan: Target common feedback errors: swapping constant levels between intervals.
Target common feedback errors: copying the right constants but attaching them to the wrong time bounds.
Target common feedback errors: omitting one interval condition or writing a condition that does not cover the plotted segment.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a piecewise definition for the graphed signal that is constant at \(2\) on \(0\le t<3\) and constant at \(-1\) on \(3\le t\le5\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to read each horizontal segment as a constant expression and pair it with the interval where that segment appears.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active conversion after the tutorial: the signal description now comes from a graph, but the expressions are constants so the only required moves are reading levels and writing interval conditions.
solution_step_plan: Identify each horizontal segment as one piece of the definition.
Read the constant height of the first segment and write it as the first expression.
Read the time interval covered by the first segment and attach it as the first condition.
Repeat the same value-and-interval pairing for the second segment.
Assemble the pieces into one brace-form definition of \(x(t)\).
practice_variation_axes: Change the constant signal levels, including negative and zero levels.
Change the interval endpoints while keeping integer breakpoints.
Use two segments by default, with occasional three-segment versions once the skill is stable.
Vary whether the graph starts at a positive, zero, or negative time.

sections.handoff_notes: The example writer should keep the graph simple and subgoal-labeled: segment, value, interval, definition. The question generator should create mirrored graph-to-piecewise conversions rather than asking for point values.

sections.section_title: Writing a Piecewise Definition from Linear Graph Segments
sections.learning_goal: Convert a graph made of straight-line signal segments into a piecewise definition by finding the formula for each line segment and assigning it to the correct time interval.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean continuous-time signal plot with two straight-line segments connecting marked points, with coordinates or gridlines sufficient to determine each segment's slope and intercept.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
marked endpoint coordinates or clear grid intersections
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use line segments whose equations can be read with low arithmetic load. Avoid curved graphs and avoid endpoint ambiguity unless that is explicitly the focus of the endpoint section.

question_policy.answer_format: A complete piecewise formula for \(x(t)\), with each linear expression paired to the correct interval inequality.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows a line segment from \((-2,0)\) to \((0,2)\), followed by a line segment from \((0,2)\) to \((3,-1)\). Write a piecewise definition for \(x(t)\).
distractor_plan: Target common feedback errors: using the endpoint value as the whole expression instead of finding the line rule.
Target common feedback errors: computing the correct slope but the wrong intercept.
Target common feedback errors: assigning a line formula to the neighboring interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a piecewise definition for the graphed signal whose first segment runs from \((-2,0)\) to \((0,2)\) and whose second segment runs from \((0,2)\) to \((3,-1)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to turn each straight segment into its own linear expression, then attach the expression to the interval covered by that segment.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The input is still a graph, but each piece now requires finding a line equation instead of copying a constant height.
solution_step_plan: Separate the graph into its straight-line pieces.
For the first segment, use two visible points to compute the slope and write the line expression.
Attach the first line expression to the first segment's time interval.
For the second segment, compute its slope and line expression from its visible endpoints.
Attach the second line expression to the second interval and combine both pieces in brace form.
practice_variation_axes: Use simple integer endpoints that give slopes such as \(1\), \(-1\), \(2\), \(-2\), or \(1/2\).
Vary the breakpoint time while keeping adjacent segments visually distinct.
Use one constant segment and one linear segment only after the pure linear case is clear.
Keep endpoint membership simple unless the question is assigned to the endpoint-condition section.

sections.handoff_notes: The example writer should explicitly label subgoals for each segment. The question generator should keep arithmetic light so the main practice remains graph-to-piecewise conversion, not algebra drill.

sections.section_title: Assigning Endpoint Conditions in a Piecewise Definition
sections.learning_goal: Use open and closed endpoint markings on a signal graph to choose the correct strict or inclusive inequalities in a piecewise definition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal plot with adjacent pieces meeting at a breakpoint where open and closed circles indicate which piece includes the boundary value.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
open circle at an excluded endpoint
closed circle at an included endpoint
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make open and closed endpoints visually unmistakable. The image should isolate endpoint membership as the new wrinkle; keep the segment formulas simple.

question_policy.answer_format: One correct symbolic piecewise definition selected from five answer choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows one piece ending with an open circle at \(t=1\) and the next piece beginning with a closed circle at \(t=1\). Select the piecewise definition whose inequalities assign \(t=1\) to the correct expression.
distractor_plan: Include a choice that reverses the open and closed endpoint inequalities.
Include a choice that uses inclusive inequalities on both adjacent pieces, causing overlap at the breakpoint.
Include a choice that uses strict inequalities on both adjacent pieces, omitting the breakpoint.
Include a choice with correct endpoint conditions but one expression assigned to the wrong interval.
Include a choice that ignores the endpoint marker and uses a generic interval convention.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Choose the piecewise definition that matches the graphed signal, paying close attention to the open and closed endpoint markings at \(t=1\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how endpoint markers determine whether each interval condition uses \(<\), \(\le\), \(>\), or \(\ge\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The formulas can remain simple, but the learner must now decide boundary membership instead of treating interval endpoints as an afterthought.
solution_step_plan: Identify the breakpoint where endpoint membership matters.
Read which graph piece has the closed endpoint at that time.
Assign the inclusive inequality to the piece that owns the closed endpoint.
Assign the strict inequality to the piece with the open endpoint.
Check that the final conditions neither overlap nor omit the boundary time unless the graph indicates that behavior.
practice_variation_axes: Move the endpoint decision to a different breakpoint.
Use left-open/right-closed and left-closed/right-open variants.
Vary whether the neighboring pieces are constant or linear while keeping their formulas simple.
Occasionally test an endpoint at the start or end of the graphed support, not only at an interior breakpoint.

sections.handoff_notes: Use symbolic answer choices, not image answer choices. The graph is the question data; the choices should differ mainly in interval inequalities and only secondarily in expressions.

sections.section_title: Writing a Piecewise Definition from Interval-Based Function Rules
sections.learning_goal: Translate a verbal or listed interval-based signal description into brace-form piecewise notation without relying on a graph.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image should be generated. The section's job is symbolic translation from interval rules into piecewise notation.

question_policy.answer_format: A complete piecewise formula for \(x(t)\) using the given function rules and interval conditions.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A signal equals \(2t+1\) for \(-1\le t<1\) and equals \(4-t\) for \(1\le t\le3\). Write \(x(t)\) in piecewise form.
distractor_plan: Target common feedback errors: copying the formulas correctly but dropping the interval conditions.
Target common feedback errors: changing the formulas while converting to brace notation.
Target common feedback errors: reversing the intervals assigned to the two function rules.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a piecewise definition for a signal that equals \(2t+1\) for \(-1\le t<1\) and equals \(4-t\) for \(1\le t\le3\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to preserve each given expression and interval condition while reorganizing the information into standard piecewise notation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The input switches from visual graph data to symbolic interval rules, so the learner must translate representation rather than infer formulas from a plot.
solution_step_plan: Identify each stated function rule as one piece of the signal.
Copy the first expression exactly and pair it with its stated interval.
Copy the second expression exactly and pair it with its stated interval.
Place the paired expressions and conditions in one brace-form definition.
Check that the written definition preserves the original endpoint conditions.
practice_variation_axes: Vary constant, linear, and simple polynomial expressions.
Vary interval endpoints and inclusion symbols.
Use descriptions written in sentences or compact rule lists.
Keep the number of pieces to two or three so representation conversion remains the focus.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should not introduce graph reading. The example writer should make the conversion feel like a reformatting-and-checking task with no hidden algebra.

sections.section_title: Adding an Otherwise Case to a Piecewise Definition
sections.learning_goal: Complete a piecewise signal definition by adding an otherwise case that covers all times not included in the explicitly stated intervals.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image should be generated. The otherwise case is a symbolic coverage decision, and a graph would shift the task away from interval coverage.

question_policy.answer_format: A complete piecewise formula for \(x(t)\) that includes an otherwise case, usually \(0\), for all remaining times.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A signal equals \(t+1\) for \(-1\le t<0\), equals \(2\) for \(0\le t\le2\), and is zero for all other times. Write a piecewise definition for \(x(t)\).
distractor_plan: Target common feedback errors: omitting the otherwise case entirely.
Target common feedback errors: writing \(0\) on only one side of the stated intervals instead of all remaining times.
Target common feedback errors: using otherwise but changing one of the explicitly stated interval rules.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a piecewise definition for a signal that equals \(t+1\) for \(-1\le t<0\), equals \(2\) for \(0\le t\le2\), and equals \(0\) for all other times.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to include the explicitly stated pieces and add a final case that covers every time not covered by those intervals.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends interval-rule translation by adding coverage outside the named intervals, a bridge toward later support and zero-region reasoning without turning this section into that later lesson.
solution_step_plan: Write the explicitly stated nonzero pieces with their given interval conditions.
Identify that the description also specifies the signal value outside those intervals.
Add a final \(0\) case using an otherwise condition or an equivalent outside-interval condition.
Check that every time either belongs to one stated interval or falls under otherwise.
Verify that endpoint conditions from the stated intervals are unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the outside value, with \(0\) as the default and occasional simple nonzero otherwise values if needed.
Use one or two explicitly stated intervals before the otherwise case.
Vary whether intervals touch or have a gap between them.
Keep formulas simple so the new cognitive load is coverage by otherwise.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not expand this into a full signal-support lesson. The focus is only on writing a complete piecewise definition whose final case covers all remaining time values.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify the support and zero regions of a continuous-time signal from a graph, formula, or piecewise definition by marking the intervals where \(x(t)\) is nonzero versus identically zero.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Signal Support and Zero Regions
sections.learning_goal: Introduce support as the time region where a signal is nonzero and zero regions as intervals where the signal is identically zero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A simple continuous-time signal plot with one highlighted nonzero interval and labeled zero regions on both sides.
visual_elements: one nonzero signal segment above the time axis
support interval highlighted with a bracket
left and right zero regions labeled on the time axis
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a clean coordinate plot with one signal trace and restrained highlighting; the image should clarify support versus zero regions without adding decorative detail.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the vocabulary and marking convention for support and zero regions before asking learners to identify them from data.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A finite-duration signal that is nonzero on one continuous interval and exactly zero everywhere outside that interval.
paragraph_plan: Start from the familiar idea that a continuous-time signal is a function of time, so each time value either has a zero or nonzero signal value.
Define support operationally as the time region where the signal is nonzero, emphasizing that the learner should mark intervals rather than describe the whole graph.
Define zero regions as intervals where the signal is identically zero, contrasting this with a signal merely touching zero at one time value.
Use the tutorial image to connect the definitions to a graph by highlighting the support interval and labeling the zero regions.
Close with the repeatable procedure: find where \(x(t)\ne 0\), write that as support, then write the remaining intervals where \(x(t)=0\) as zero regions.
display_math_plan: \\text{zero region: an interval on which } x(t)=0 \\text{ for every } t

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section definitional and procedural; do not introduce topic sequencing, convolutions, or advanced support conventions.

sections.section_title: Identifying Support from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Identify the support of a graphed signal by locating exactly where the graph is nonzero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal graph that is zero outside one finite interval and nonzero throughout that interval.
visual_elements: clear left and right support boundaries
optional open or closed endpoint markers if endpoints matter
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The graph is the problem data. Generate simple finite-duration signal plots with readable integer boundary times and no extra labels that reveal the answer.

question_policy.answer_format: one support interval or union of intervals in interval notation
question_policy.practice_question_model: The graph of \(x(t)\) is nonzero only from \(t=-2\) to \(t=3\) and is zero elsewhere. What is the support of \(x(t)\)?
distractor_plan: Offer the zero regions instead of the support.
Shift one endpoint by one grid mark.
Reverse the interval endpoints.
Include the entire displayed time window instead of only the nonzero part.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The graph of \(x(t)\) is shown. Identify the support of \(x(t)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to read the nonzero time interval directly from a signal graph and state it as the support.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active use of the tutorial procedure, with the learner reading the support from a visual signal rather than from a stated definition.
solution_step_plan: Point to the portions of the graph that lie away from the time axis.
Mark the first and last time values where the nonzero portion occurs.
Write the marked nonzero interval as the support.
Check that all times outside the stated support have \(x(t)=0\).
practice_variation_axes: move the support interval left or right
change the support duration
use one or two nonzero pieces
vary endpoint inclusion only when the graph clearly marks endpoints

sections.handoff_notes: Keep answer choices symbolic; do not make learners choose among graph thumbnails because the target move is reading support from one graph.

sections.section_title: Identifying Zero Regions from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Identify the zero regions of a graphed signal by locating intervals where the graph is identically on the time axis.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal graph with one finite nonzero interval and visible left and right intervals where the signal lies on the time axis.
visual_elements: flat zero portions on the time axis
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The zero portions must be visually clear as intervals on the time axis. Avoid curves that only touch the axis unless the section is explicitly about isolated zeros.

question_policy.answer_format: a union of zero-region intervals in interval notation
question_policy.practice_question_model: The graph of \(x(t)\) is nonzero for \(-1<t<2\) and is zero everywhere else on the displayed time line. Which intervals are zero regions of \(x(t)\)?
distractor_plan: Give the support interval instead of the zero regions.
List only one of the two outside zero regions.
Include the nonzero interval as part of the zero regions.
Use endpoint inclusion that conflicts with the graph markers.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The graph of \(x(t)\) is shown. Identify the zero regions of \(x(t)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate how to read intervals where the graph is identically zero and state them as zero regions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This uses the same kind of graph as the support example but asks for the complement: the intervals where the signal is zero rather than nonzero.
solution_step_plan: Locate the nonzero part of the signal to avoid including it in a zero region.
Identify each interval where the graph lies on the time axis.
Write the left and right zero regions separately or as a union.
Check that every time in each stated interval has \(x(t)=0\).
practice_variation_axes: shift the nonzero interval
change whether zero regions appear on one side or both sides
use finite displayed windows with clear outside-zero behavior
vary endpoint markers when visually unambiguous

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example tightly paired with the previous section so the only new demand is switching from support to zero regions.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Piecewise Definition
sections.learning_goal: Find support and zero regions by scanning the cases of a piecewise definition and separating zero-valued cases from nonzero-valued cases.

question_policy.answer_format: support and zero regions written as interval notation
question_policy.practice_question_model: For \(x(t)=0\) when \(t<-1\), \(x(t)=2\) when \(-1\le t<2\), \(x(t)=0\) when \(2\le t<4\), \(x(t)=-1\) when \(4\le t\le 5\), and \(x(t)=0\) when \(t>5\), which choice gives the support and zero regions?
distractor_plan: Swap the support intervals with the zero regions.
Merge two nonzero intervals across an internal zero region.
Omit the internal zero region.
Use endpoint inclusions that do not match the piecewise inequalities.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the given piecewise definition of \(x(t)\), identify the support and the zero regions.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to classify each piecewise case as zero or nonzero and then combine the corresponding intervals.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This removes the graph and requires the same support-versus-zero decision from symbolic interval conditions.
solution_step_plan: Read each row of the piecewise definition with its time condition.
Label each row as zero-valued or nonzero-valued.
Combine the nonzero-valued intervals to form the support.
Combine the zero-valued intervals to form the zero regions.
Preserve open and closed endpoints from the original inequalities.
practice_variation_axes: change the number of piecewise rows
include or remove an internal zero interval
vary open and closed endpoints
use constant or simple nonzero expressions in the nonzero rows

sections.handoff_notes: Do not introduce graphing as a required intermediate step; the point is to read support and zero regions directly from symbolic cases.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Formula
sections.learning_goal: Find support and zero regions from a compact formula by identifying where the formula is explicitly active and where the signal is defined to be zero.

question_policy.answer_format: support and zero regions written as interval notation
question_policy.practice_question_model: A signal is given by \(x(t)=3e^{-t}\) for \(0\le t\le 4\) and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise. Which choice gives the support and zero regions of \(x(t)\)?
distractor_plan: Treat the decaying exponential as if it eventually becomes exactly zero.
Ignore the stated active interval and give all real numbers as the support.
Give only one outside zero region.
Use endpoint inclusions inconsistent with the stated formula interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A signal is given by \(x(t)=2e^{-t}\) for \(0\le t\le 4\) and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise. Identify the support and the zero regions of \(x(t)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to use the active interval of a compact formula to identify where the signal is nonzero and where it is zero by definition.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This compresses the piecewise information into a formula plus an otherwise-zero statement, so the learner must not rely on row-by-row scanning.
solution_step_plan: Identify the interval on which the nonzero formula applies.
Verify that the formula is not zero on that interval.
State that active interval as the support.
Use the otherwise-zero statement to write the zero regions outside the support.
Check endpoint inclusion against the stated formula interval.
practice_variation_axes: change the active interval
use a different always-nonzero formula on the active interval
change endpoint inclusions
place the active interval away from the origin

sections.handoff_notes: Avoid unit-step notation unless it is already established elsewhere in the module; keep formulas readable as active interval plus otherwise-zero statements.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Isolated Zeros from Zero Regions
sections.learning_goal: Distinguish a single time where \(x(t)=0\) from an interval where \(x(t)\) is identically zero.

question_policy.answer_format: classification of isolated zeros and zero-region intervals
question_policy.practice_question_model: A signal is given by \(x(t)=t-1\) for \(-1\le t\le 3\) and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise. Which statement correctly identifies the zero regions and explains the zero at \(t=1\)?
distractor_plan: Call the isolated zero time a zero region.
Merge the two outside zero regions through the isolated zero.
Remove the active interval from the support because it contains one zero value.
Treat every solution of \(x(t)=0\) as an interval where the signal is identically zero.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A signal is given by \(x(t)=t\) for \(-2\le t\le 2\) and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise. Identify the zero regions, and decide whether \(t=0\) is a zero region.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a single zero value inside an otherwise active signal is an isolated zero, not an interval where the signal is identically zero.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds one conceptual wrinkle to formula-based support: the active formula can equal zero at one point without creating a zero region.
solution_step_plan: Identify the outside intervals where the signal is defined to be zero.
Solve the active formula for any time values where it equals zero.
Classify the outside intervals as zero regions because the signal is identically zero there.
Classify the single active-interval zero as an isolated zero, not a zero region.
State the support or nonzero portions without confusing an isolated zero with an interval of zero signal.
practice_variation_axes: move the isolated zero within the active interval
use a different linear active formula
change the outside zero intervals
ask for the classification before asking for interval notation

sections.handoff_notes: This section should protect the key distinction: zero regions require intervals of identically zero signal, while isolated zeros are individual time values.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a continuous-time signal from its graph or piecewise definition as even, odd, or neither by comparing \(x(t)\) with \(x(-t)\) over matching positive and negative time regions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Even and Odd Signal Symmetry
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that even and odd symmetry are whole-signal tests based on comparing \(x(t)\) with \(x(-t)\) at matching positive and negative times.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A compact coordinate-plane comparison figure with three small continuous-time signal sketches: an even signal mirrored across the vertical axis, an odd signal with origin symmetry, and a neither signal with one mismatched positive-negative pair. Mark matching sample locations \(t\) and \(-t\) on each sketch.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use simple piecewise-linear signals with integer tick marks and uncluttered labels. The image should support the rule comparison, not add decorative context.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define even, odd, and neither classifications and show that the decision depends on checking corresponding values at \(t\) and \(-t\) across the full signal.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one positive time and its matching negative time on a graph, comparing equal heights for even symmetry and opposite-signed heights for odd symmetry.
paragraph_plan: Introduce symmetry as a rule for comparing a signal value at a positive time with the value at the matching negative time.
State the even-symmetry rule and connect it to vertical-axis mirror symmetry on a graph.
State the odd-symmetry rule and connect it to equal magnitude with opposite sign on matching time points.
Explain that a signal is neither if the full set of matched time pairs fails both tests.
Set up the upcoming examples as repeated classification decisions from graphs first, then from a piecewise definition.
display_math_plan: Neither: the signal does not satisfy either relationship for all matching time values.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial as minimum effective direct instruction: define the two tests, show the visual meaning, and avoid turning the introduction into a full classification procedure.

sections.section_title: Identifying Even Symmetry from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Classify a graph as even by verifying that matching positive and negative time values have the same signal value.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A graph of a continuous-time signal with clear vertical-axis mirror symmetry, such as a triangular pulse centered at \(t=0\) with matching heights at \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\).
visual_elements: matched positive and negative time ticks
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The worked example and practice questions need graph images as the task data. Use simple integer coordinates so the comparison \(x(t)=x(-t)\) is visually checkable.

question_policy.answer_format: one classification label: even, odd, or neither
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify the graphed continuous-time signal as even, odd, or neither by comparing its values at matching positive and negative times.
distractor_plan: Include odd as a distractor for students who see symmetry but ignore that the heights have the same sign.
Include neither as a distractor for students who check only one side of the graph or miss the vertical-axis mirror relationship.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether the signal shown in the graph is even, odd, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate a graph-based even classification by comparing several matched time pairs and concluding that the graph satisfies \(x(-t)=x(t)\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from definition to the first full classification task, using a graph where every matched pair has equal height.
solution_step_plan: Identify matched time pairs on opposite sides of the vertical axis.
Compare the signal heights at each matched pair.
State that the heights are equal for the checked pairs and that the graph mirrors across the vertical axis.
Conclude that the signal is even.
practice_variation_axes: Use a different symmetric pulse shape.
Vary the support width while keeping the graph centered at zero.
Use flat, triangular, or curved segments as long as vertical-axis symmetry is clear.

sections.handoff_notes: The section should build automaticity around the even test, not introduce odd-versus-neither ambiguity beyond the final classification choice.

sections.section_title: Identifying Odd Symmetry from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Classify a graph as odd by verifying that matching positive and negative time values have equal magnitude and opposite sign.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A graph of a continuous-time signal with origin symmetry, passing through the origin, with positive values for positive time and corresponding negative values for negative time.
visual_elements: matched positive and negative time ticks
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use graph data where the sign reversal is visible at multiple matched time pairs. Keep the plot simple enough that students compare values rather than infer from visual complexity.

question_policy.answer_format: one classification label: even, odd, or neither
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify the graphed continuous-time signal as even, odd, or neither by checking whether matched positive and negative times have opposite-signed values.
distractor_plan: Include even as a distractor for students who recognize symmetry but do not check the sign change.
Include neither as a distractor for students who overfocus on a discontinuity or shape change while the matched values still satisfy the odd rule.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether the signal shown in the graph is even, odd, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate an odd classification by showing that each matched negative-time value is the negative of the corresponding positive-time value.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Changes the comparison from equal heights to opposite-signed heights while keeping the task graph-based.
solution_step_plan: Choose matched time pairs on the positive and negative sides of the graph.
Compare each pair's magnitude and sign.
Check that \(x(0)=0\) when the graph includes the origin.
State that the matched values satisfy \(x(-t)=-x(t)\).
Conclude that the signal is odd.
practice_variation_axes: Use different odd-symmetric piecewise-linear shapes.
Vary positive-side amplitudes while matching negative-side sign reversals.
Include examples that pass through the origin clearly.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that odd symmetry is not visual sameness across the vertical axis; the decisive cue is equal magnitude with opposite sign at matched times.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Neither Even Nor Odd Symmetry
sections.learning_goal: Classify a graph as neither by finding matched time values that fail both the even and odd symmetry tests.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A graph of a continuous-time signal with one or more asymmetric matched time pairs, such as unequal same-sign values at \(t=1\) and \(t=-1\) and no consistent sign reversal across the origin.
visual_elements: matched positive and negative time ticks
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The graph should contain at least one clear positive-negative time pair that rules out even symmetry and odd symmetry. Avoid making the failure depend on tiny visual differences.

question_policy.answer_format: one classification label: even, odd, or neither
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify the graphed continuous-time signal as even, odd, or neither by identifying a matched time pair that fails both symmetry rules.
distractor_plan: Include even as a distractor when part of the graph appears mirrored but at least one matched pair has unequal same-sign values.
Include odd as a distractor when one pair has opposite signs but the full graph does not satisfy \(x(-t)=-x(t)\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether the signal shown in the graph is even, odd, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate that a single well-chosen counterexample pair can rule out both even and odd classifications.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the negative case: instead of confirming a symmetry, the learner must reject both tests using matched time pairs.
solution_step_plan: Pick a matched pair of time values with clearly readable graph heights.
Compare the values to test whether they are equal.
Compare the values to test whether they are negatives of each other.
Use the failed pair to rule out even and odd symmetry.
Conclude that the signal is neither.
practice_variation_axes: Use support mismatch on one side of the origin.
Use unequal positive and negative side amplitudes.
Use a graph where one local feature looks symmetric but another pair breaks the rule.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the reasoning controlled: students should not scan vaguely for asymmetry; they should name a matched pair and apply both tests.

sections.section_title: Classifying Symmetry from a Piecewise Definition
sections.learning_goal: Classify a piecewise-defined signal by substituting \(-t\), matching the relevant intervals, and comparing the result with \(x(t)\) and \(-x(t)\).

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the task data should be a compact piecewise definition.

question_policy.answer_format: one classification label: even, odd, or neither
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify the piecewise-defined signal as even, odd, or neither by comparing the expression on a positive-time interval with the expression on the corresponding negative-time interval.
distractor_plan: Include even as a distractor when students compare interval shapes but miss a sign change in the formula.
Include odd as a distractor when students see opposite-side intervals but do not verify \(x(-t)=-x(t)\).
Include neither as a distractor when students mishandle the interval mapping under \(t\mapsto -t\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Classify \(x(t)=\begin{cases}2+t,& -2\le t<0\\2-t,& 0\le t\le 2\\0,& \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\) as even, odd, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to classify symmetry from notation by mapping positive-time values to the corresponding negative-time rule and comparing the expressions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from graph inspection to symbolic interval matching while preserving the same \(x(t)\) versus \(x(-t)\) decision.
solution_step_plan: Identify the positive-time interval and the matching negative-time interval.
Evaluate the negative-time rule at \(-t\) for a positive \(t\) in the matching interval.
Compare the resulting expression with the positive-time expression.
Check the outside-support rule for matched times.
Conclude whether the signal is even, odd, or neither.
practice_variation_axes: Use different matching interval endpoints.
Vary between constant and linear pieces.
Include outside-support cases where both sides are zero.
Include formulas that are close to even or odd but fail one interval comparison.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should not ask the writer to graph the signal. The important controlled wrinkle is translating the same symmetry test into interval and formula comparisons.

entries.lesson_title: Basic Signal Parameters: Amplitude, Offset, and Duration
entries.lesson_core_move: Extract amplitude, vertical offset, and duration from graphical or piecewise continuous-time signal descriptions by identifying extrema, baseline level, and nonzero support interval.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Basic Signal Parameters: Amplitude, Offset, and Duration
sections.learning_goal: Define amplitude, vertical offset, and duration as graph-readable parameters of a continuous-time signal and establish a fixed extraction order.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean continuous-time signal plot with axes labeled t and x(t), a finite-duration active portion, visible maximum and minimum active levels, a center or baseline level, and two support endpoints.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
finite-duration signal with zero value outside its support
visible maximum and minimum levels on the active portion
baseline or center-level marker for vertical offset
horizontal bracket marking duration across the support interval
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use one simple annotated signal plot to reduce cognitive load; labels should clarify the three parameters without adding decorative detail.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that amplitude comes from vertical variation, vertical offset comes from the baseline or center level, and duration comes from the length of the nonzero support interval.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A finite-duration signal whose active portion has a clear maximum, minimum, baseline or center level, and start and end time.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the three parameters as compact descriptors of how tall the signal is, where it is centered vertically, and how long it lasts.
Define amplitude as the vertical distance from the baseline or center level to an extremum, using half the peak-to-peak range when both maximum and minimum are visible.
Define vertical offset as the baseline or center level about which the active part of the signal is shifted.
Define duration as the end time minus the start time over the interval where the signal is nonzero.
Give the operational extraction order: identify active extrema, identify the baseline or center level, locate the nonzero support endpoints, then report amplitude, offset, and duration.
display_math_plan: If the active portion has maximum M and minimum m, use A = (M - m)/2 for amplitude and C = (M + m)/2 for vertical offset.
If the nonzero support is [t_start, t_end], use D = t_end - t_start for duration.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section concise and directive. The goal is to establish vocabulary and extraction order, not to make students infer the definitions by discovery.

sections.section_title: Finding Amplitude from Signal Extrema
sections.learning_goal: Extract amplitude from a graph by reading the active maximum and minimum levels and converting peak-to-peak range into distance from the center level.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal plot whose active portion has a clearly readable maximum value of 4 and minimum value of -2, with axes and gridlines sufficient to read the extrema.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
gridlines or tick marks at the relevant y-values
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For practice variants, change only the active maximum and minimum values while keeping the graph easy to read from the grid.

question_policy.answer_format: numeric amplitude
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows a continuous-time signal whose active portion has maximum value 5 and minimum value -1. What is the signal's amplitude?

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph shown to find the amplitude of the continuous-time signal.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the amplitude is half the vertical distance between the active maximum and active minimum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active extraction task and isolates amplitude before asking for offset or duration.
solution_step_plan: Read the maximum active signal value from the graph.
Read the minimum active signal value from the graph.
Compute the peak-to-peak range as maximum minus minimum.
Divide the peak-to-peak range by 2 and report the nonnegative amplitude.
practice_variation_axes: Use zero-centered and vertically shifted active signals.
Vary the maximum and minimum values while keeping them on clear gridlines.
Keep the task focused on amplitude only.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not let the worked example become a full three-parameter extraction. The only target is translating extrema into amplitude.

sections.section_title: Finding Vertical Offset from the Baseline Level
sections.learning_goal: Extract vertical offset from a graph by identifying the baseline or center level of the active signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal plot whose active portion ranges from 1 to 5 with a visually clear center or baseline level at x(t) = 3.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
active signal segment with readable high and low levels
gridlines or tick marks at the relevant y-values
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The section image may show a subtle baseline marker; question images should preserve enough visual information to infer the offset without explicitly labeling the answer.

question_policy.answer_format: numeric vertical offset
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows a continuous-time signal whose active portion has maximum value 6 and minimum value 2. What is the signal's vertical offset?

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph shown to find the vertical offset of the continuous-time signal.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the vertical offset is the center level halfway between the active maximum and active minimum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds baseline recognition after amplitude extraction while still using the same extrema-reading habit.
solution_step_plan: Read the active maximum and minimum levels from the graph.
Identify the center level halfway between those extrema.
Compute the offset as the average of the maximum and minimum levels.
State the vertical offset with its sign.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive, zero, and negative offsets.
Keep the active maximum and minimum symmetric around an easy center level.
Avoid mixing in duration until the learner can identify offset reliably.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that offset is a vertical location, not the signal height or peak-to-peak range.

sections.section_title: Finding Duration from the Nonzero Support Interval
sections.learning_goal: Extract duration from a graph by locating the interval where the signal is nonzero and subtracting the start time from the end time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A continuous-time signal plot that is zero outside the interval from t = -1 to t = 4 and nonzero on that interval, with support endpoints readable from the time axis.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
zero-valued signal outside the active interval
tick marks at the support start and end times
image_policy.image_generation_notes: For question images, vary support endpoints while keeping the zero and nonzero regions visually unambiguous.

question_policy.answer_format: numeric duration
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows a continuous-time signal that is nonzero only from t = 2 to t = 7. What is the signal's duration?

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph shown to find the duration of the continuous-time signal.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that duration is the length of the nonzero support interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This shifts from vertical parameter extraction to time-interval extraction while keeping the graph-reading format familiar.
solution_step_plan: Locate the first time where the signal becomes nonzero.
Locate the last time where the signal returns to zero.
Subtract the start time from the end time.
Report the result as a positive duration.
practice_variation_axes: Use support intervals that start at negative, zero, and positive times.
Use integer and simple fractional endpoints.
Keep open or closed endpoint details from becoming the main task because they do not change the interval length in this lesson.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep support detection visual and concrete. Do not introduce energy, period, or time scaling.

sections.section_title: Extracting All Three Parameters from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Extract amplitude, vertical offset, and duration together from one graph by coordinating extrema, baseline, and nonzero support information.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A finite-duration continuous-time signal plot with zero value outside [-2, 3], active high level 6, active low level 2, and center level 4, all readable from gridlines.
visual_elements: coordinate axes labeled t and x(t)
zero-valued signal outside the support interval
image_policy.image_generation_notes: The visual should provide all data needed for the three parameters, but question images should not label amplitude, offset, or duration directly.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered triple (amplitude, vertical offset, duration)
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows a finite-duration signal that is nonzero from t = 1 to t = 6, has active maximum value 5, active minimum value 1, and center level 3. Find its amplitude, vertical offset, and duration.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the graph shown to find the amplitude, vertical offset, and duration of the continuous-time signal.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate the full extraction routine on one graph and report the three parameters in a consistent order.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This combines the three previously isolated extraction moves without changing representation.
solution_step_plan: Identify the active maximum and active minimum values.
Compute amplitude from half the active peak-to-peak range.
Compute vertical offset from the midpoint of the active maximum and minimum.
Identify the start and end of the nonzero support interval.
Compute duration and report all three parameters in the requested order.
practice_variation_axes: Vary active extrema and support endpoints together.
Use vertical offsets that are not zero.
Keep each graph visually simple enough that the challenge is coordination, not deciphering a complicated plot.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the synthesis graph section. The writer should explicitly model an orderly scan of the graph rather than jumping to answers.

sections.section_title: Extracting All Three Parameters from a Piecewise Definition
sections.learning_goal: Extract amplitude, vertical offset, and duration from a piecewise continuous-time signal definition by reading active extrema and support endpoints from the formula conditions.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered triple (amplitude, vertical offset, duration)
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given x(t) = 0 for t < 1, x(t) = t + 1 for 1 <= t < 3, x(t) = 7 - t for 3 <= t <= 5, and x(t) = 0 for t > 5, find the amplitude, vertical offset, and duration.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given x(t) = 0 for t < -2, x(t) = t + 4 for -2 <= t < 0, x(t) = 4 - t for 0 <= t <= 2, and x(t) = 0 for t > 2, find the amplitude, vertical offset, and duration.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to extract the same three parameters from symbolic interval conditions and active formulas without drawing a graph.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This changes the representation from graph to piecewise definition while preserving the same three-parameter extraction routine.
solution_step_plan: Use the piecewise conditions to identify the nonzero support interval.
Evaluate the active formula pieces at the relevant endpoints and join point to find the active minimum and maximum values.
Compute amplitude from half the active peak-to-peak range.
Compute vertical offset from the midpoint of the active maximum and minimum.
Compute duration from the support interval endpoints and report the three parameters in order.
practice_variation_axes: Use simple piecewise-linear active definitions with integer endpoint values.
Vary the support interval without introducing new signal operations.
Keep the symbolic formulas easy enough that parameter extraction remains the main skill.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not ask for plotting here. The point is to transfer the graph-based extraction routine to a compact piecewise definition.
